children: Boeing’s

hopes for a fresh wave of aircraft orders from China are fading ahead of Thursday’s meeting between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the negotiations.
Instead of securing commitments for hundreds of additional jets, Boeing
is focused on completing a previously announced agreement for China to buy 200 aircraft. The deal emerged from the Trump-Xi summit in May and marked an important reopening of a market where Boeing
had been largely shut out since 2017.
For Boeing

investors, completing the 200-plane agreement would still provide valuable backlog and strengthen the company’s position in a strategically important aviation market. But the absence of a larger follow-on order would temper expectations that improving U.S.-China relations could quickly translate into a major commercial windfall. China is expected to require roughly 9,000 new aircraft through 2045, making access to the market important to Boeing’s long-term competition with Airbus.
Expectations come down
Before the May summit, Boeing

and government officials had discussed a potential Chinese purchase of as many as 500 aircraft. The eventual 200-plane agreement was smaller, though Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg subsequently indicated that the order could represent the beginning of additional business.

Those expectations have since cooled. Ortberg last week cautioned against assuming another major order was imminent, while people familiar with the negotiations told Reuters that talks remain unsettled.

Attention at Thursday’s summit is expected to center on broader U.S.-China issues, including extending a trade truce, artificial intelligence safeguards, Taiwan, soybean exports and rare earth minerals.
There could still be progress on the existing Boeing

agreement. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said this week that about 140 aircraft orders were in relatively advanced stages, with another 10 being finalized. Reuters reported that portions of the May agreement could be announced during the summit if contracts are completed.
Airbus gains ground
Boeing’s long absence from significant Chinese orders has benefited Airbus
, which has expanded its presence in the country and operates an aircraft final-assembly line in Tianjin.
Political tensions haven’t been Boeing’s only obstacle. The company’s production and quality problems have also complicated its effort to regain momentum internationally.

China had previously sought assurances that aircraft purchased from Boeing would continue receiving engines, spare parts and other components despite trade disputes. Chinese officials said in May that the U.S. had provided supply assurances as part of the agreement.
For Boeing, Thursday’s summit may therefore be less about landing another blockbuster order than ensuring the 200-aircraft deal already announced makes it across the finish line.

title: Boeing’s hopes for bigger China jet deal fade ahead of Trump-Xi summit
